title: Identifying materials by their properties
objective: Use measured physical properties to identify an unknown material.
question: Can a material be identified from its mass and volume?
dependentVariable: Mass and volume of the sample
procedure: Weigh the sample on the Precision Balance and record the mass.
Fill the Graduated Cylinder with water, add the same sample and record the volume it displaces.
Open the journal: density is calculated and compared with reference values.
expected: Each pure material has a characteristic density; mixtures fall between the densities of their components.
interpretation: If the measured density agrees with a reference value within the measurement uncertainty, that material is a likely match. Two materials with similar densities need a second test (for example a spectrum).
limitations: Density alone cannot prove identity. Porous or water-absorbing samples give wrong volumes.

title: Measuring density
objective: Determine the density of a solid from independent measurements of mass and volume.
question: What is the density of iron, and how certain is the value?
procedure: Measure the mass (±0.01 g).
Measure the displaced volume (±0.2 mL).
Calculate ρ = m/V and its uncertainty.
expected: Iron: about 7.87 g/cm³. Larger samples give smaller relative uncertainty in volume.
interpretation: The relative uncertainty of the density is dominated by the volume reading, because the balance is far more precise than the cylinder.
limitations: Displacement assumes the sample is not porous and does not dissolve.

hypothesis.prompt: Which will have the higher density: an iron ingot or the raw iron ore it came from?

title: Separating a mixture by filtration
objective: Separate an insoluble solid from a liquid.
question: How can sand (or another insoluble solid) be removed from water?
procedure: Add water and an insoluble solid to the Reaction Vessel.
Use the Filter action.
Insoluble solids remain on the filter; dissolved substances pass through with the water.
expected: Insoluble particles are trapped; dissolved salt or sugar passes through.
interpretation: Filtration separates by particle size, so it cannot separate a solution: dissolved ions and molecules are far smaller than the filter pores.
limitations: The game recovers solids completely; real filtration loses some material.

title: Separating a solution by distillation
objective: Recover pure water and salt from seawater.
question: Can dissolved salt be separated from water?
materials: Seawater (fill a beaker in an ocean)
procedure: Place seawater on the Laboratory Heater with a Condenser above it.
Heat until the water boils (just above 100 °C, because dissolved salt raises the boiling point).
Collect distilled water from the Condenser; salt crystals remain in the heater.
expected: Water vapour leaves; salt does not evaporate at 100 °C.
interpretation: Distillation separates by differences in boiling point. Evaporation alone recovers the salt but loses the water.
limitations: Real distillation also carries over small amounts of volatile impurities.

title: Observing a phase change
objective: Observe how temperature behaves while water boils.
question: What happens to the temperature of water while it boils?
procedure: Heat water on the Laboratory Heater with a Data Recorder attached.
Watch the temperature–time graph.
Keep heating after boiling starts.
expected: The temperature rises, then stays at about 100 °C while the water boils away.
interpretation: During boiling, energy breaks intermolecular attractions (latent heat) instead of raising the temperature, giving a plateau on the graph.
limitations: The game assumes 1 atm pressure. At high altitude water boils at a lower temperature.

hypothesis.prompt: Once the water is boiling and you keep heating, the temperature will…

options.text: It will stay the same (within measurement uncertainty)

title: Investigating thermal insulation
objective: Compare cooling rates with and without an insulating jacket.
question: Does insulation change how fast hot water cools?
procedure: Heat water to about 70 °C, switch the heater off and record the cooling curve.
Repeat with a wool jacket fitted.
Compare the slopes of the two graphs.
expected: The insulated sample cools more slowly.
interpretation: Insulation lowers the overall heat-loss coefficient UA, reducing the rate of heat transfer to the surroundings.
limitations: Cooling rate also depends on temperature difference, so compare slopes at similar temperatures.

hypothesis.prompt: With a wool jacket, the cooling rate will…

options.text: It will stay the same (within measurement uncertainty)

title: Comparing heat transfer through materials
objective: Compare how different jacket materials conduct heat.
question: Which materials are good thermal insulators?
materials: Wool, glass, bricks or an iron block as jackets
procedure: Record cooling curves with at least two different jacket materials.
Compare the cooling rates in the journal.
expected: Wool insulates best; metals conduct heat quickly.
interpretation: Materials with low thermal conductivity (wool, trapped air) slow heat flow; metals, with free electrons, conduct heat well.
limitations: Jackets are modelled by their thermal conductivity and a fixed thickness.

title: Conservation of mass
objective: Test whether mass changes during a chemical reaction.
question: Does the total mass change when calcite reacts with acid?
procedure: Seal the Reaction Vessel with its stopper.
Add calcite powder and acid; record the starting mass.
Let the reaction finish and compare the final mass.
Repeat with the vessel open.
expected: Sealed: mass stays the same. Open: mass decreases because carbon dioxide escapes.
interpretation: Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, so the total mass of a closed system is constant. An apparent loss means something (here, gas) left the system.
limitations: Real sealed vessels can leak or burst under gas pressure; the game vessel is ideal.

hypothesis.prompt: In a sealed vessel, the total mass after the reaction will…

options.text: It will stay the same (within measurement uncertainty)

title: Investigating acidity and pH
objective: Measure the pH of acidic and basic solutions.
question: How acidic or basic are common laboratory solutions?
materials: Vinegar, hydrochloric acid, sodium hydroxide solution, limewater
procedure: Use the pH Meter on beakers or vessels containing different solutions.
Record at least one acid and one base.
Try neutralising an acid with a base in the Reaction Vessel.
expected: Acids: pH below 7; bases: pH above 7; neutralisation moves the pH towards 7.
interpretation: pH is logarithmic: each unit is a tenfold change in hydrogen-ion concentration. Weak acids (vinegar) have higher pH than strong acids at the same concentration.
limitations: The pH model uses ideal-solution concentrations at 25 °C.

hypothesis.prompt: When sodium hydroxide is added to hydrochloric acid, the pH will…

options.text: It will stay the same (within measurement uncertainty)

title: Constructing a simple circuit
objective: Make a lamp light using a complete circuit.
question: What does a circuit need for current to flow?
procedure: Connect the battery's + and − terminals to the lamp with copper wire, forming a loop.
Close the switch.
Measure the current with the Multimeter.
expected: The lamp lights only when there is a complete loop.
interpretation: Charge flows only around a closed path. The battery provides the potential difference; the lamp converts electrical energy to light and heat.
limitations: The lamp is modelled as a fixed resistance; a real filament's resistance rises as it heats up.

title: Comparing series and parallel circuits
objective: Compare currents and brightness in series and parallel arrangements.
question: How does adding a second lamp change the circuit?
procedure: Build two lamps in series and measure the current.
Build two lamps in parallel and measure the current from the battery.
expected: Series: dimmer lamps, smaller current. Parallel: full brightness, larger total current.
interpretation: Resistances in series add (R = R₁ + R₂); in parallel the combined resistance is smaller (1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂).
limitations: Wires have small but real resistance in the model; battery internal resistance slightly reduces the voltage under load.

hypothesis.prompt: Adding a second lamp in parallel, the total current from the battery will…

options.text: It will stay the same (within measurement uncertainty)

title: Testing Ohm's law
objective: Show that current through a resistor is proportional to voltage.
question: Is V/I constant for a resistor?
procedure: Build a circuit containing a resistor.
Use the Multimeter on the resistor to measure V and I.
Compare V/I with the resistor's labelled value.
expected: V/I equals the resistance.
interpretation: For an ohmic conductor the I–V graph is a straight line through the origin whose slope is 1/R.
limitations: Resistors are ideal (temperature-independent) in the model.

title: Investigating reflection and refraction
objective: Measure angles of reflection and refraction.
question: How does light change direction at a mirror and at a water surface?
procedure: Use the Optical Bench mirror mode and vary the angle.
Switch to refraction mode and compare air→water and air→glass.
Find the critical angle going from glass to air.
expected: Reflection angle equals incidence angle; refracted rays bend towards the normal entering a denser medium.
interpretation: Light travels more slowly in water and glass; Snell's law describes the change of direction at the boundary.
limitations: Ray optics ignores diffraction and the wave nature of light.

title: Measuring the motion of a cart
objective: Measure the acceleration of a cart on a ramp.
question: How does ramp angle affect acceleration?
procedure: Set an angle on the Motion Track and release the cart.
Read the distance–time and speed–time graphs.
Repeat at different angles.
expected: Steeper ramps give larger accelerations: a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ).
interpretation: The speed–time graph is a straight line whose slope is the acceleration; the distance–time graph is a parabola.
limitations: Air resistance and rolling resistance beyond the friction coefficient are ignored.

title: Calculating mechanical energy
objective: Compare potential energy lost with kinetic energy gained.
question: Where does the energy of a rolling cart go?
procedure: Run the cart with friction set to zero and compare Eₚ lost with Eₖ gained.
Increase friction and repeat.
expected: Without friction Eₖ = Eₚ; with friction some energy becomes heat.
interpretation: Energy is conserved; friction converts some mechanical energy into internal (thermal) energy.
limitations: Rotational kinetic energy of wheels is ignored.

title: Using a microscope
objective: Observe the microscopic structure of samples.
question: What do ordinary materials look like at high magnification?
materials: Sand, salt, sugar, leaves, kelp, feathers, bone meal
procedure: Place a sample on the Microscope stage.
Adjust the focus and note the scale bar.
Compare crystals, cells and fibres.
expected: Crystals have regular shapes; living tissues are made of cells.
interpretation: A compound microscope multiplies the magnification of the objective and eyepiece lenses.
limitations: The images are illustrations generated for the game, not photographs.

title: Pressure and temperature of a gas
objective: Observe how gas pressure changes with temperature at constant volume.
question: What happens to the pressure in a sealed vessel when it is heated?
procedure: Seal the Reaction Vessel on a Laboratory Heater.
Record the pressure at two temperatures at least 20 K apart.
expected: Pressure increases in proportion to absolute temperature (Gay-Lussac's law).
interpretation: At constant volume P/T is constant for an ideal gas: faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often.
limitations: Water vapour pressure is not included in the headspace model.

title: Comparing electrical conductivity
objective: Classify materials as conductors or insulators.
question: Which materials conduct electricity?
materials: Copper ingot, iron ingot, glass, quartz, diamond...
procedure: Use the conductivity probe mode of the Material Analyzer on several samples.
Find at least one conductor and one insulator.
expected: Metals conduct; most minerals and glass do not.
interpretation: Metals have delocalised electrons that carry current; in ionic and covalent solids the electrons are bound.
limitations: Resistivities are typical room-temperature values; real samples vary with purity.

title: Efficiency of a simple machine
objective: Measure the efficiency of a ramp used to raise a load.
question: How much of the work done pushing a cart up a ramp is stored as potential energy?
procedure: Use push mode to drag the cart up the ramp at constant speed.
Compare the work done with the potential energy gained.
expected: Efficiency is below 100 % whenever there is friction.
interpretation: A ramp reduces the force needed but not the energy: friction makes the input work larger than the output.
limitations: Constant-speed pushing (no kinetic energy change) is assumed.

title: Plotting and interpreting data
objective: Plot experimental data and find a best-fit line.
question: What can the slope of a graph tell us?
procedure: Attach a Data Recorder to a working machine.
Collect at least 5 points.
Open the graph and read the best-fit slope, intercept and R².
expected: The slope gives a rate (for example K/s while heating).
interpretation: A straight-line fit summarises a linear relationship; R² near 1 indicates the line describes the data well.
limitations: Least-squares fits assume random, independent errors.

title: Electrolysis and Faraday's law
objective: Split water with electricity and relate the gas produced to the charge passed.
question: How much hydrogen does a given charge produce?
procedure: Fill the Electrolysis Station with water and connect it to a battery.
Let current flow and read the charge passed and the gas collected.
expected: Twice as much hydrogen as oxygen by moles; n(H₂) = Q/(2F).
interpretation: Each H₂ molecule needs two electrons, so the amount of gas is proportional to the charge.
limitations: 100 % current efficiency is assumed.

title: Emission spectroscopy
objective: Identify elements from their emission lines.
question: Which elements are present in a sample?
procedure: Analyse a sample in the Material Analyzer's spectrum mode.
Match the lines with the reference database.
expected: Each element shows its own set of lines (for example sodium at 589 nm).
interpretation: Electrons in excited atoms drop to lower energy levels and emit photons with energies characteristic of each element.
limitations: Line intensities are simplified; some elements' strongest lines lie outside the visible range.

title: Testing for carbon dioxide
objective: Use limewater to detect carbon dioxide.
question: Is the gas produced by acid and calcite carbon dioxide?
procedure: Make limewater from slaked lime and water in a sealed Reaction Vessel.
Add calcite powder and acid so CO₂ is produced inside.
expected: The limewater turns milky.
interpretation: CO₂ reacts with dissolved calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate.
limitations: Both reactions happen in one vessel in the game; in a real lab the gas is bubbled through limewater in a separate tube.
